title: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
summary: Compute edit distances with the Wagner-Fischer table, compare Damerau, Indel, Jaro-Winkler, trigram and token scores, and see how trigram indexes, BK-trees, Levenshtein automata and SymSpell avoid full scans.
outcomes: Compute a Levenshtein distance by filling the Wagner-Fischer table and tracing back the edits
Explain how OSA, true Damerau-Levenshtein and Indel distance differ, and why fuzz.ratio is Indel based
Compute Jaro-Winkler and trigram Jaccard scores and predict which pairs each metric misjudges
Explain how trigram indexes, BK-trees, Levenshtein automata and SymSpell avoid comparing against every string
Choose a scorer, threshold policy and index for search, database lookup, spelling correction or record matching

lessons.title: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts

blocks.md:
A user types `recieve` into a search box. A recruiter searches for `google` while the profile says `Google LLC`. A product feed lists `Acme Corp` and another lists `Corp Acme`. Exact equality says none of these match, and even a substring test such as SQL `LIKE '%recieve%'` finds nothing, because the typo is *inside* the word.

Fuzzy matching replaces the yes or no test with a number: a **distance** (how many changes separate two strings, lower is closer) or a **similarity** (a score, usually from 0 to 1 or 0 to 100, higher is closer). You then match when the number passes a threshold, or rank candidates by it.

The classic distance counts **edits**, where one edit is a single-character change:

- **insertion**: add a character (`sic` to `sick`)
- **deletion**: remove a character (`black` to `lack`)
- **substitution**: replace one character with another (`box` to `fox`)

The **Levenshtein distance** between two strings is the minimum number of these edits needed to turn one into the other. It is named after Vladimir Levenshtein, whose paper appeared in Russian in 1965 and in English in 1966.

blocks.title: Three edits turn kitten into sitting

scenes.caption: Line the two words up column by column. The dash marks a position where kitten has no character. Most columns already agree.
Columns 1 to 3 and 5 agree, so they cost nothing. Column 0 needs a substitution (k to s): 1 edit so far.
Column 4 needs a second substitution (e to i). Two edits so far.
Column 6 inserts g. Total: 3 edits. No shorter sequence exists, so the Levenshtein distance is 3. Lesson 2 shows how to prove that without guessing alignments.

blocks.prompt: What is the Levenshtein distance between `form` and `from`? A person sees one mistake: two letters swapped.
blocks.reveal: **2**, not 1. Levenshtein has no swap operation, so the cheapest fix is two substitutions (o to r, r to o). Swapped adjacent letters are one of the most common typing errors, which is why lesson 3 adds a **transposition** edit.

blocks.md:
Levenshtein distance has properties you will rely on later:

- $d(x,x)=0$ and $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ (symmetric).
- **Triangle inequality**: $d(x,z) \le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Together these make strings with this distance a *metric space*, which lesson 5 exploits to prune a search.
- **Length bounds**: $|\,|x|-|y|\,| \le d(x,y) \le \max(|x|,|y|)$. You need at least one insertion or deletion per character of length difference, and you never need more edits than the longer string has characters.

A raw distance is hard to threshold. Two edits between `lewenstein` and `levenshtein` (11 characters) is a near match; two edits between `ab` and `abcd` changes half the string. So libraries also report a **normalized similarity** that divides by the largest possible distance:

blocks.caption: For kitten and sitting: 1 - 3/7 = 0.571. For lewenstein and levenshtein: 1 - 2/11 = 0.818. For ab and abcd: 1 - 2/4 = 0.5.

blocks.md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

blocks.question: A search box accepts any dictionary word within 2 Levenshtein edits of the query. For which query is this rule most likely to return junk?
options: All three are equally safe because the threshold is the same
blocks.explain: Two edits can rewrite 2 of the 3 letters of `cat`, so `cut`, `bag`, `act` and many other 3-letter words all match. For a 10 or 11 letter word, 2 edits keep most of the string intact. This is why search engines scale the allowed edits with term length (lesson 6).

blocks.question: You know $d(a,b)=1$ and $d(b,c)=2$ under Levenshtein distance. What does the triangle inequality tell you about $d(a,c)$?
options: It is at most 3, and at least 1
Nothing, because edit distance is not a metric
blocks.explain: The triangle inequality gives the upper bound $d(a,c) \le 1+2 = 3$. Applied the other way, $d(b,c) \le d(b,a)+d(a,c)$, so $d(a,c) \ge 2-1 = 1$. These two bounds are exactly what a BK-tree uses in lesson 5 to skip whole subtrees.

lessons.title: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell

blocks.md:
Trying every possible sequence of edits is exponential. The fix is **dynamic programming**: solve the problem for every pair of *prefixes*, smallest first, and reuse the answers. Define $D[i][j]$ as the edit distance between the first $i$ characters of $a$ and the first $j$ characters of $b$. The answer is the bottom-right cell $D[|a|][|b|]$.

This algorithm was discovered independently many times; it carries the name of Wagner and Fischer, who published it in 1974 as the string-to-string correction problem.

blocks.tex: D[i][j] = \min\begin{cases} D[i-1][j] + 1 & \text{delete } a_i \\ D[i][j-1] + 1 & \text{insert } b_j \\ D[i-1][j-1] + [a_i \ne b_j] & \text{match or substitute} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The bracket is 1 when the characters differ and 0 when they match. Base cases: D[i][0] = i (delete all i characters) and D[0][j] = j (insert all j characters).

blocks.md: Read each cell as: the best way to align these two prefixes must end with one of three moves. Coming **from above** means the last character of $a$ was deleted. Coming **from the left** means the last character of $b$ was inserted. Coming **diagonally** means the two last characters were aligned, for free if they are equal and for 1 if not. Every cell depends only on its upper, left and upper-left neighbours, so you can fill the table row by row.

blocks.prompt: In the table below, cell $D[2][2]$ compares `ki` with `si`. The last characters match (i and i), and $D[1][1]=1$. What value goes in $D[2][2]$?
blocks.reveal: **1**. When the last characters match, the diagonal move costs nothing, so $D[2][2]=D[1][1]+0=1$. The other two moves give $D[1][2]+1=3$ and $D[2][1]+1=3$. The only edit needed so far is the k to s substitution.

blocks.title: Levenshtein table for kitten (rows) vs sitting (columns)

scenes.caption: Base cases first. Row ε is the cost of building each prefix of sitting from nothing (j insertions); column ε is the cost of deleting each prefix of kitten (i deletions).
Row k. Cell (k, s): k differs from s, so take 1 + min(0, 1, 1) = 1. The rest of the row grows by one per column: each extra letter of sitting must be inserted.
Row i. Cell (i, i) matches, so it copies its diagonal neighbour: D[2][2] = D[1][1] = 1. A match never adds cost.
Rows t and t. Both cells on the diagonal match again, so kitt vs sitt still costs only 1 (the k to s substitution).
Row e. Cell (e, i): the letters differ. Diagonal gives 1 + 1 = 2, above gives 2 + 1 = 3, left gives 2 + 1 = 3. The minimum is 2: a second substitution.
Row n. Cell (n, n) matches, so it copies 2 from the diagonal. The last cell (n, g) is cheapest from the left: 2 + 1 = 3, meaning insert g. The distance is 3.
Traceback: follow the moves that produced each minimum back from the corner. The path is diagonal (k to s, then four free matches with e to i in between) and one step left (insert g).

blocks.caption: Each row needs only the previous one, so memory is two rows. Time is proportional to the number of cells, |a| x |b|.

blocks.md:
The cost is $O(|a|\cdot|b|)$ time. For two 10-character names that is 100 cells, which is nothing. Comparing one query against a million names is a million tables, which is why lessons 5 and 6 are about *not* doing that.

When you only care whether $d \le k$, two shortcuts apply. First, $D[i][j] \ge |i-j|$, so only the band of cells within $k$ of the diagonal can hold a value $\le k$, and you can skip the rest. Second, the minimum of a row never decreases from one row to the next, so once a whole row exceeds $k$ you can stop early. Libraries such as RapidFuzz use a `score_cutoff` argument to pick these faster paths.

The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

blocks.question: A teammate initializes the first row as `prev = [0] * (len(b) + 1)` instead of `list(range(len(b) + 1))`. What does the function now compute?
options: The same Levenshtein distance, because row 0 is overwritten anyway
The cost of matching `a` against the best substring of `b` that ends at its last character, because skipping a prefix of `b` becomes free
blocks.explain: Row 0 says how much it costs to consume a prefix of `b` before `a` starts. Setting it to 0 makes that free, so a match may start anywhere in `b`. Sellers used exactly this change in 1980 to turn the distance algorithm into approximate substring search. It is a useful algorithm, but not Levenshtein distance.

blocks.question: You only accept matches with at most 1 edit. The query has 6 characters and a candidate has 9. How much of the DP table must you fill to reject the candidate?
options: Only the diagonal band of width 3
None: the length difference already proves the distance is at least 3
blocks.explain: Every character of length difference needs at least one insertion or deletion, so $d \ge 9-6 = 3 > 1$. A length check is the cheapest filter of all and real implementations apply it before touching the table.

lessons.title: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer

blocks.md: Which operations you allow, and what each costs, is a modelling choice. Fred Damerau's 1964 study of spelling errors found that about 80 percent of misspellings can be fixed by a single insertion, deletion, substitution, or **transposition** (swapping two adjacent characters). Plain Levenshtein charges 2 for a transposition, so `form` vs `from` scores like two unrelated typos.

The cheapest way to add swaps to the table is **optimal string alignment (OSA)**: one extra case in the recurrence. If the last two characters of each prefix are each other's swap, you may jump back two rows and two columns for a cost of 1.

blocks.tex: \text{if } a_i = b_{j-1} \text{ and } a_{i-1} = b_j:\quad D[i][j] = \min\big(D[i][j],\; D[i-2][j-2] + 1\big)
blocks.caption: Applied after the three usual moves, for i, j at least 2.

blocks.title: form (rows) vs from (columns): Levenshtein, then OSA

scenes.caption: Plain Levenshtein. Cell (r, o) compares for with fro and holds 2: two substitutions. The final distance is 2.
OSA. At cell (r, o), the last two letters are o r in form and r o in from: a swap. The new case takes D[1][1] + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1.
The cheaper cell flows to the corner: (m, m) matches and copies the diagonal, so the OSA distance is 1.

blocks.md:
OSA has a catch: it never edits the same substring twice. RapidFuzz's docs show the difference: `OSA.distance("CA", "ABC")` is 3, but `DamerauLevenshtein.distance("CA", "ABC")` is 2. True Damerau-Levenshtein swaps CA to AC and then inserts B between the swapped letters; OSA is not allowed to touch that pair again.

This also means OSA is **not a metric**: $d(\text{CA},\text{AC})=1$ and $d(\text{AC},\text{ABC})=1$, yet $d(\text{CA},\text{ABC})=3 > 1+1$. Lucene's `FuzzyQuery` documents its measure as "Damerau-Levenshtein (optimal string alignment)", so in practice the name often means OSA.

Going the other way, the **Indel distance** allows only insertions and deletions, each costing 1. A substitution then costs 2 (delete plus insert), and the distance equals the number of characters not in a longest common subsequence. RapidFuzz describes Indel as Levenshtein with weights (1, 1, 2), and the Jurafsky and Martin textbook uses the same substitution-costs-2 convention. RapidFuzz's popular `fuzz.ratio` is a normalized Indel similarity:

blocks.caption: Docs example: 'this is a test' vs 'this is a test!' needs 1 insertion over 14 + 15 = 29 characters, so 100 x 28/29 = 96.55. kitten vs sitting: Indel 5, ratio 100 x (1 - 5/13) = 61.54.

blocks.title: Four distances on the same pairs

scenes.caption: kitten vs sitting: two substitutions and an insertion. Indel pays 2 per substitution, so it reports 5.
form vs from: a single swap. Only the transposition-aware measures call it 1 edit.
recieve vs receive, the classic typo: also a swap (ie vs ei), so OSA and Damerau-Levenshtein say 1 while Levenshtein says 2.
CA vs ABC: OSA cannot insert between swapped letters, so it reports 3 while true Damerau-Levenshtein reports 2.

blocks.md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

blocks.question: What is `fuzz.ratio("test", "tent")` in RapidFuzz?
options: 50.0, because two of the four letters differ
75.0, because the substitution costs 2 Indel edits over 8 characters
25.0, because only one letter is wrong
blocks.explain: Indel has no substitution, so s to n is a deletion plus an insertion: 2 edits. The lengths sum to 8, so ratio = 100 x (1 - 2/8) = 75. The 87.5 answer assumes a substitution costs 1, which is Levenshtein, not Indel.

blocks.question: You are building a structure whose correctness depends on the triangle inequality (lesson 5). Which distance is unsafe to plug in?
blocks.explain: OSA violates the triangle inequality: CA to AC is 1, AC to ABC is 1, but CA to ABC is 3. A search structure that prunes with that inequality could skip a real match. Levenshtein, Indel and true Damerau-Levenshtein are metrics.

lessons.title: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs

blocks.md: Edit distances treat every position alike and care about word order. Real data breaks both assumptions. People rarely mistype the first letters of a name, and `Corp Acme` is the same company as `Acme Corp` even though Levenshtein needs 8 edits. Three other families of scores handle these cases: **Jaro-Winkler** for short names, **character n-grams** for order-tolerant matching, and **token-based** scorers for multi-word strings.

**Jaro similarity** comes from record linkage, where it was used to match names across census files. Two characters *match* if they are equal and no further apart than $\lfloor \max(|s_1|,|s_2|)/2 \rfloor - 1$ positions. Let $m$ be the number of matches. Walk the matched characters of each string in order; each position where they differ is half a **transposition**, and $t$ is the number of such positions divided by 2. William Winkler's 1990 paper then boosts the score when the strings share a prefix, because agreement at the start is strong evidence for names.

blocks.caption: J = 0 when m = 0. Here l is the common prefix length, capped at 4, and p = 0.1 is the prefix scale from Winkler (1990).

scenes.caption: Both strings have 6 characters, so the match window is floor(6/2) - 1 = 2: a character may match one up to 2 positions away.
All 6 characters find a partner within the window (t at 3 matches t at 4, h at 4 matches h at 3). So m = 6.
Matched characters in order: m a r t h a vs m a r h t a. Two positions disagree, so t = 2/2 = 1. J = (6/6 + 6/6 + 5/6)/3 = 0.9444.
Common prefix mar has length 3, so JW = 0.9444 + 3 x 0.1 x (1 - 0.9444) = 0.9611. The shared start pushes the score up.

blocks.md: Implementations differ in details Winkler's paper leaves open. RapidFuzz's `JaroWinkler` uses `prefix_weight=0.1` by default (allowed 0 to 0.25), caps the prefix at 4, and in its source only applies the boost when the Jaro score is above 0.7.

**Trigram similarity** (PostgreSQL's `pg_trgm`) breaks each string into three-character pieces. It lowercases, ignores non-alphanumeric characters, and pads each word with two spaces in front and one behind, so `cat` becomes `"  c"`, `" ca"`, `"cat"`, `"at "`. The similarity is the **Jaccard index** of the two trigram sets: shared trigrams divided by distinct trigrams in either. Because sets ignore order, `Acme Corp` and `Corp Acme` have identical trigram sets and score 1.0. The `%` operator matches when similarity exceeds `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold`, which defaults to 0.3.

blocks.caption: pg_trgm docs example: word vs words share 4 of 7 distinct trigrams, similarity 0.571429.

blocks.md: **Token scorers** in RapidFuzz work on words. `token_sort_ratio` sorts the words of each string and then runs `ratio`. `token_set_ratio` compares the shared words with the leftovers and returns 100 when one string's word set is a subset of the other's. `partial_ratio` slides the shorter string along the longer one and keeps the best `ratio`. None of the scorers lowercase by default (`processor=None`): `ratio("Google LLC", "google")` is 62.5, and 75.0 after `utils.default_process`, which lowercases, strips non-alphanumerics and trims.

blocks.prompt: Before you step through the chart: for `Acme Corp` vs `Corp Acme`, which of the six scores will be lowest?
blocks.reveal: **Normalized Levenshtein, at 11.1.** Character by character the strings line up badly, so it needs 8 edits over 9 characters. Trigram Jaccard, `token_sort_ratio` and `token_set_ratio` all give 100 because they ignore word order. No single metric wins every pair; the chart shows each one failing somewhere.

blocks.title: Six scores (0 to 100) on six pairs, after default_process

scenes.caption: recieve vs receive. Jaro-Winkler likes the long shared prefix (96.7). Trigram Jaccard is only 33.3: the swap destroys every trigram in the middle of the word.
Google LLC vs google. token_set_ratio gives 100 because {google} is a subset of {google, llc}. Character metrics charge for the missing suffix.
Acme Corp vs Corp Acme. Order-blind scores (trigrams, token sort, token set) give 100; Levenshtein gives 11.1.
Dwayne vs Duane, a name pair from Winkler's paper. Jaro-Winkler 84.0 is the most forgiving; trigrams give 18.2 because short words have few trigrams.
Austria vs Australia: different countries, yet Jaro-Winkler gives 92.7 and fuzz.ratio 87.5. High similarity is not the same as the same entity.
New York Mets vs New York Yankees: different teams. token_set_ratio still gives 76.2 from the shared words new york. Thresholds must be tuned on labelled pairs from your data.

blocks.md: `partial_ratio` produces false positives on short strings: `fuzz.partial_ratio("ai", "said hello")` is 100 because `ai` appears inside `said`. Likewise `token_set_ratio` returns 100 for any subset, so `google` vs `google cloud platform team` is a perfect score. Use these scorers with a minimum length or combine them with other evidence.

blocks.question: Using the Jaro-Winkler formula with p = 0.1: `dwayne` vs `duane` has Jaro similarity 0.8222 and shares only the first letter. What is the Jaro-Winkler score?
options: 0.8222, because a prefix of 1 earns no boost
blocks.explain: JW = J + l x p x (1 - J) = 0.8222 + 1 x 0.1 x 0.1778 = 0.8400. Every shared leading character (up to 4) moves the score a tenth of the remaining distance toward 1.

blocks.question: You match company names where one source often adds suffixes such as LLC or Inc and words are sometimes reordered. Which scorer handles both cases, and what must you watch for?
options: fuzz.ratio; it is the most precise
partial_ratio; it finds the best substring
token_set_ratio; it ignores order and extra words, but any subset scores 100, so very short names can match too much
blocks.explain: token_set_ratio ignores word order and scores 100 when one word set contains the other, which absorbs added suffixes. The same property means a one-word name like `google` scores 100 against any longer name containing it, so pair it with a length check or a second score.

lessons.title: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees

blocks.md:
Everything so far compares one pair. A real lookup compares one query against a whole column or dictionary, and running the DP table against a million names per keystroke is too slow. Indexes avoid it in two ways:

1. **Filter then verify**: a cheap index proposes a small set of candidates that *might* be close, then the exact score runs only on those.
2. **Prune with the triangle inequality**: organize strings by their distances to each other so whole groups can be ruled out without comparing against them.

The filter idea rests on the **q-gram lemma**. One edit can destroy at most $q$ of a string's overlapping q-grams (the ones that cover the edited position). A string of length $m$ has $m-q+1$ q-grams, so any string within $k$ edits of it still shares at least $m-q+1-kq$ of them. For `recieve` ($m=7$, $q=3$, $k=1$) that is $5-3=2$ unpadded trigrams; `relieve`, one edit away, shares exactly two (`iev`, `eve`). A string that shares fewer than the bound cannot be within $k$ edits and is skipped without computing a distance.

PostgreSQL builds this with a **GIN** index (`gin_trgm_ops`), an inverted index from each trigram to the rows containing it, or a **GiST** index (`gist_trgm_ops`), which stores each row's trigram set as a bitmap signature. A query extracts its own trigrams, reads only the matching posting lists, and rechecks similarity on the candidates. Below, the query `recieve` has 8 padded trigrams; the chart shows ten dictionary words.

blocks.title: Step 1: shared trigrams read from the posting lists

scenes.caption: Each of the 8 query trigrams has a posting list; counting hits per word gives these overlaps. banana shares none and is never touched. In a large dictionary most rows share nothing with the query.

blocks.title: Steps 2 and 3: score and rank the candidates

scenes.caption: Step 2: compute the Jaccard similarity (x100) for the nine candidates only. Four words reach the default threshold of 30: relieve 45.5, retrieve 41.7, recipe 36.4, receive 33.3.

Step 3: rank. The intended word receive comes last of the four, because the ie swap breaks the middle trigrams. Rerank with an edit distance: OSA puts receive and relieve level at 1 edit, ahead of retrieve and recipe at 2.

blocks.caption: Patterns from the pg_trgm documentation. The same trigram indexes also accelerate LIKE, ILIKE and regular-expression searches.

blocks.md: The second idea is the **BK-tree** of Burkhard and Keller (1973), probably the first general structure for searching a metric space. Pick any string as the root. Every other string goes into the child subtree labelled by its distance to the root, and the same rule applies recursively. To find everything within radius $r$ of query $q$: compute $d = d(q, \text{node})$, report the node if $d \le r$, and descend only into children whose label $i$ satisfies $d-r \le i \le d+r$. The triangle inequality guarantees that every skipped subtree holds only strings farther than $r$.

blocks.title: BK-tree search for cape within 1 edit

scenes.caption: Ten words inserted in the order book, books, cake, boo, boon, cook, cape, cart, bolt, look. Each edge label is the Levenshtein distance from child to parent.
Compare cape with the root: d(cape, book) = 4. With r = 1 only children labelled 3 to 5 can hold a match, so only the edge labelled 4 is followed.
Six words are ruled out without computing their distance. Next, d(cape, cake) = 1, which is within the radius: cake is a result. Children labelled 0 to 2 may hold matches, so both are visited.
d(cape, cape) = 0 is a match; d(cape, cart) = 2 is not. Result: cake and cape, found with 4 distance computations instead of 10.

blocks.prompt: Same tree, query `bool` with radius 1. Its distance to the root `book` is 1. How many of the ten words must be compared?
blocks.reveal: **7.** With $d=1$ and $r=1$, children labelled 0 to 2 qualify, so `books` (1) and `bolt` (2) are followed and only the `cake` subtree (3 words) is skipped. Results: book, boo and boon. Pruning works best when the query is far from a node relative to $r$; a query close to the root prunes little.

blocks.md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

blocks.question: In a BK-tree, the query is at distance 3 from a node and the search radius is 1. Which child subtrees are searched?
blocks.explain: Any match $u$ in a child labelled $i$ has $d(u,\text{node}) = i$ and $d(q,u) \le 1$, so by the triangle inequality $|i-3| \le 1$, giving $i \in \{2,3,4\}$. Every other child provably contains no match.

blocks.question: A trigram index returns `receive` as a candidate for `recieve`, but ranks it below `relieve`. What is the best fix?
options: Rerank the candidates the index returns with an edit distance that counts transpositions
blocks.explain: The index did its job: receive is in the candidate set. Its ordering reflects trigram overlap, which a swap in the middle of a word damages. Reranking with OSA or Damerau-Levenshtein lifts receive (1 edit) into a tie with relieve (also 1 edit, a substitution), ahead of retrieve and recipe (2 edits); a tie-breaker such as word frequency then decides. Lowering the threshold only adds candidates, and longer grams are damaged even more by a swap.

lessons.title: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production

blocks.md: Search engines face the dictionary version of the problem: find every indexed *term* within $k$ edits of a query term. Before Lucene 4.0, `FuzzyQuery` did the obvious thing: visit every unique term in the index, compute its edit distance, and keep the close ones. Lucene 4.0 replaced that with a **Levenshtein automaton**: a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that accepts exactly the strings within $k$ edits of the query term, built with the construction of Schulz and Mihov ([Fast string correction with Levenshtein automata](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10032-002-0082-8), 2002). Lucene intersects that automaton with the sorted term dictionary, so it seeks and scans only the regions that can still match. Michael McCandless's write-up of the change is titled *Lucene's FuzzyQuery is 100 times faster in 4.0*.

The intuition comes straight from the DP table. Fix the query and read a candidate one character at a time; after each character the current DP row summarizes everything that matters about the prefix read so far. That row is the automaton's **state**. If every entry in the row exceeds $k$, no continuation can bring the distance back down, so every term with this prefix is rejected at once. In a sorted dictionary, all terms sharing a prefix sit next to each other, so the whole block is skipped.

blocks.title: Reading terms against the query fuzzy with k = 1

scenes.caption: The start state is row 0 of the table: the cost of matching each prefix of fuzzy against nothing.
Read j. The row minimum is 1, which is still within k = 1, so keep reading.
Read a. Every entry is now at least 2, so no term starting with ja can be within 1 edit of fuzzy. Reject after 2 characters, and skip every other ja term too.
Now fuzz. The rows stay on the diagonal: after f, u, z, z the row is [4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1]. The last entry is 1, so fuzz is accepted (one insertion of y).
scenes.output:
jazzy: rejected after 2 of 5 characters
fuzz: accepted, distance 1

blocks.title: A sorted term dictionary scanned for fuzzy with k = 1

scenes.caption: Brute force (Lucene before 4.0): read every character of every term and finish its full DP table: 58 rows for these 12 terms.
Automaton style: stop each term as soon as its state dies. gauzy and jazzy die after 2 characters; funny, furry and fuss after 4. Matches: fuzz, fuzzy, muzzy.
Simplified: Lucene precomputes the states into DFA tables and seeks through its term dictionary, so blocks of terms behind a dead prefix are skipped without being read at all.

blocks.md: Elasticsearch's `fuzzy` query exposes this machinery. Its docs describe `fuzziness` as a maximum Levenshtein edit distance, with transpositions counted as one edit by default (`transpositions: true`). The recommended value `AUTO` (equivalent to `AUTO:3,6`) scales edits with term length: terms of 0 to 2 characters must match exactly, 3 to 5 allow one edit, and longer terms allow two. `max_expansions` (default 50) caps how many matching terms are used, and `prefix_length` (default 0) requires the first characters to match exactly, which shrinks the search. Lucene's `FuzzyQuery` supports at most 2 edits, and its javadoc warns that higher distances match a large part of the term dictionary.

blocks.caption: recieve has 7 characters, so AUTO allows 2 edits. With transpositions on, receive is only 1 edit away.

blocks.md: **SymSpell** (Wolf Garbe) takes a different route for spelling correction against a fixed dictionary: the *symmetric delete* algorithm. Offline, it generates every string reachable by deleting up to $k$ characters from each dictionary word and stores them in a hash map. At query time it generates the deletes of the query and looks them up. Insertions, substitutions and transpositions on the query side all show up as deletes on one side or the other, so only deletes are ever generated: a 5-letter word has 25 deletes within 3 edits. Candidates are then verified with an actual edit distance computation.

blocks.title: Symmetric delete with k = 1: one-character deletes

scenes.caption: Each row lists the 7 strings made by deleting one character. The dictionary rows were computed in advance and stored in a hash map from delete to word.
Lookup: receve and recive appear in both the query row and the receive row. A shared delete on both sides covers a substitution or, as here, a transposition.

reieve is shared with relieve (substitute c with l). Both candidates are verified with the real distance: receive is 1 (a swap) and relieve is 1 (a substitution). Among the closest, SymSpell prefers the most frequent word.

blocks.md: Choose the structure by the job. A search engine field: Elasticsearch or Lucene `fuzzy` with `AUTO`. A database column: `pg_trgm` with a GIN or GiST index, then rerank. Single-word spelling correction against a fixed dictionary: SymSpell or a Levenshtein automaton. Matching names or records: normalize, block candidates cheaply, then score with Jaro-Winkler or RapidFuzz token scorers using thresholds tuned on labelled pairs.

Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

blocks.question: With Elasticsearch `fuzziness: AUTO` (default 3,6), how many edits are allowed for the terms `ox`, `cat` and `kitchen`?
blocks.explain: AUTO:3,6 means lengths 0 to 2 must match exactly, 3 to 5 allow one edit, and more than 5 allow two. `ox` has 2 characters (0 edits), `cat` 3 (1 edit), `kitchen` 7 (2 edits).

blocks.question: A Levenshtein automaton for query `fuzzy` with k = 1 reaches a state where every entry of the DP row is 2 after reading `ja`. Why can it reject every term starting with `ja` without reading further?
options: Because terms starting with ja are rare
Because the row minimum never decreases as more characters are read, so the final distance will be at least 2
Because the automaton only accepts terms of exactly 5 characters
blocks.explain: Each new cell is at least the minimum of the previous row (diagonal moves add 0 or 1, the others add 1), so a row whose minimum is 2 can only lead to distances of 2 or more. That dead state lets the engine skip the entire ja block of the sorted term dictionary.

blocks.question: SymSpell with k = 1 finds that the query and a dictionary word share a one-character delete, while neither is a delete of the other. What kind of single error explains that?
options: A substitution or an adjacent transposition
Nothing; it is a false positive that cannot be within 1 edit
blocks.explain: A shared one-character delete fits one differing position (a substitution, like reieve from recieve and relieve) or an adjacent swap (receve from recieve and receive). It does not guarantee 1 edit: abc and bca share the delete bc but are 2 edits apart, so SymSpell verifies every candidate with a real distance.
